title: Network Security — Practice Exam 1
description: Firewalls, common network attacks, and IPsec VPNs.

questions.question: What does this rule do on a Linux host?
options: Silently discards incoming TCP traffic to port 22
Discards outgoing TCP traffic to port 22
Refuses incoming SSH connections with an ICMP error
questions.explanation: The rule is appended (-A) to the INPUT chain, matches TCP traffic to destination port 22 (SSH), and jumps to DROP, which discards packets without replying. REJECT, not DROP, would send an error back, so option D is wrong.

questions.question: A stateless packet filter keeps track of TCP connections, so it can allow reply packets only for connections that were opened from inside.
questions.explanation: Tracking connections is what a stateful firewall does. A stateless filter judges each packet on its own header fields, with no memory of earlier packets.

questions.question: Which attack sends many TCP SYN segments to a server and never completes the handshake, filling its table of half-open connections?
questions.explanation: A SYN flood leaves each connection half-open, so the server keeps state for every one until its backlog is full. DNS amplification is also a denial of service, but it floods the victim with large DNS replies instead of exhausting connection state.

questions.question: Which IPsec protocol provides confidentiality by encrypting the payload?
questions.explanation: ESP encrypts the payload and can also authenticate it. AH authenticates packets but does not encrypt anything, which makes it the most tempting wrong answer.

questions.question: An attacker can use ARP spoofing to redirect traffic of hosts on a different subnet, on the far side of a router.
questions.explanation: ARP works only inside one broadcast domain, and routers do not forward ARP messages. ARP spoofing affects hosts on the attacker's own local network.

questions.question: In IPsec tunnel mode with ESP, the whole original IP packet, including its header, is encrypted and placed inside a new IP packet.
questions.explanation: Tunnel mode wraps the entire original packet in a new outer IP header, so the inner addresses are hidden. Transport mode protects only the payload and keeps the original header.

questions.question: A firewall checks these rules from top to bottom and applies the first one that matches. A packet arrives for 10.0.0.5 on TCP port 80. What happens to it?
questions.code:
Rule 1: allow tcp  any -> 10.0.0.5 port 443
Rule 2: deny  ip   any -> any
options: It is allowed, because no rule names port 80
It is dropped without matching any rule
It is allowed by an implicit default rule
questions.explanation: Rule 1 matches only port 443, so the packet falls through to rule 2, which denies all IP traffic. Option A is tempting because the address matches rule 1, but the port does not.

questions.question: What kind of scan does this command run?
options: A TCP SYN (half-open) scan of ports 1 to 1024
questions.explanation: -sS sends a SYN and reads the reply without completing the handshake, which is why it is called half-open. A full connect scan is -sT, so option A is wrong.

questions.question: What is the main job of IKE (Internet Key Exchange) in IPsec?
options: Negotiating security associations and the keys they use
Assigning IP addresses to VPN clients
questions.explanation: IKE sets up the security associations: it authenticates the peers and agrees on algorithms and keys. The packets themselves are then protected by ESP or AH, so option A describes ESP, not IKE.

questions.question: A DMZ puts public-facing servers in a network segment separate from the internal network.
questions.explanation: A DMZ (demilitarized zone) lets outside users reach public servers while a firewall keeps those servers apart from internal hosts, so a compromised web server does not give direct access to the internal network.
